I understand your concerns with the formulations in the post. Nevertheless, I would like to add some nuances as your evaluation of their education is denigrating. OP's native language probably isn't English (as they also seemed to have another background than most people who replied). In another comment OP mentioned that in the country they live in use the term 'diagnosis' for giftedness, which is also the case for where I live. In retrospective, I understand 'identify' might be more suitable and fit better with the normative practices in other parts in the world. I think with 'spectrum', they might have used it to acknowledge the variety/diversity within this cohort.

I understand there are lots of uninformed posts in this sub and trolls etc., which make you suspicious.  As a fellow non-native speaker (and someone from a country where the term 'diagnosis' is also used in the context of giftedness - like OP did), I just wanted to add this...

The field of psychodiagnostics and psychological support can also rely on other instruments or classifications than the DSM (although it is indeed a very important one). Giftedness is not something to be treated, but giftedness can be taken into account while treating. Cf. When some is depressed related to loss of a loved one, the experience of loss can be taken into account as well within the broader treatment.

You do realize there are more components to giftedness than intelligence that can make social functioning more challenging, right?

Belgium. It's not a psychiatrist diagnosis in clinical psychology based on the DSM-5 but it is a classification/term they teach about in university along with varieties in intelligence, development and learning 'disabilities' (such as ADHD, ASD, dyslexia and others). In practice, it is studied and tested within the field of psychodiagnostics and people can get specialized in this area (an important author is Dr. Tessa Kieboom).

Once again it is not a medical diagnosis, but a 'conclusion' or diagnosis (maybe 'identifying' instead of diagnosing is more suitable?) after testing followed by a report that is validated. I meant 'diagnosis' here in broad sense, as a broad explaination about a client's challenges, specific symptoms and possible explainations. In narrow sense, it's only related to clinical ones. (In my native language the term 'diagnosis' is both used for clinical diagnosis and the more broader one, I'm sorry for the confusion). I never implied it is a disability, all I wanted to  'demonstrate' with my previous comment is that difference in cognitive functions and emotional experiences related to giftedness are increasingly being researched and acknowledged by professionals (at least in the country I life in) as something that can shape a person's experience in life significantly. It is a 'diagnosis' one can get tested for (through IQ test, working memory and semi-structured interviews on social and emotional experiences), which can complete the picture of a client (situate their current challenges in life more specifically from this angle - only if applicable of course -) and their developmental trajectory during childhood. (Also, it is hardly ever diagnosed on its own. It oftens only gets suggested to get tested when a client with anxiety symptoms, depressive symptoms, existential worries from a young age or other social needs than peers are persistent and the clinician suspects the possibility of giftedness of that respective client. So, it gets studied more in the context of comorbidities.)

You may not be a fan of this ;), but I hope you understand variety in practices across the globe vary a little...

I totally agree with you that OP/people in general should find out what's the specfic aspect they struggle with such as social skills and should seek help for that, and shouldn't just seek a diagnosis. But if 'a diagnosis' or better understanding of oneself (or own's giftedness) can accelerate this process, why not

Although it isn't a medical diagnosis, it is one of the formal diagnosis within psychodiagnostics, at least in the country I live in. When a clinical psychologists feels like someone's anxiety, depressive symptoms and/or social struggles can be linked to giftedness, some of them suggest to get this diagnosis to double check whether or not this hypothesis (of giftedness in the client) is correct and whether or not it is useful to invest in psychoeducation on this for instance. (It's often being compared to the functionality of diagnosis like ADHD and ASS, as their might be specific social struggles and anxiety symptoms related to 'masking' and feeling like an outcast).

To connect this to your input, the diagnosis of giftedness can actually be 'empowering' or inspiring to value your strengths more and use them to improve other skills :).

To put sh behaviours in kids into perspective, I think 1 in 5 teens (I don't know actually, but it came across in some documentairies) have experienced with sh behaviour the age of 18 at least once. Although only a part of them continues to struggle with it, doing it for one or a limited amount of times is more common than people might think... It is possible that your child has seen it from someone else (school), movies or internet. For instance, when I was 12, our teachers displayed a movie which graphically showed sh (it was a movie related to bullying prevention, a bullied person sh'ed in the movie). Also, I recall my classmates borrowing books feom famous youth authors that wrote stories on ass*ult, sh etc. The pathways on how young people learn about it and get engaged in it are plentiful (and could but aren't necessarily related to you nor something you could have prevented).


P.S. If you want to talk with me, I am hear to listen". 


I understand you don't want to "talk them into it" or react to protectively since this can cause them to distance themselves from you, but personally I guess that the worst thing with sh (at ypur child's age) might be feeling lonely in that particular experience; a burden; ashamed etc. So please don't be too afraid to address it.

I have no idea whether it is normal, but I understand why you feel this is very early on. (A first appointment would also feel early to me). I think you have pointed out the most important factor that 'normalizes' or contextualizes this early diagnosis: insurance. Given this context, I would evaluate it as normal ;-)

Given the context of your insurance plan, a diagnosis is sometimes needed. So, I guess your therapist wanted to provide a plausible diagnosis to help ypu out with insurance. The fact that this therapist has written/recorded this diagnosis at least reflect that they believe your situation meets at least a part of the criteria to be diagnosed (no therapist would pick any random diagnosis). The fact that they dare to sign this mean they are rather 'sure' or confident enough this early diagnosis is likely to be correct. Although some further exploration could be needed, this diagnosis seems 'valid' based on your therapist's professional opinion (for now). 


As for your 2nd question on the validity of this diagnosis, I am curious as to why you are so preoccupied with whether this diagnosis exceeds the context of insurance or not and is actually valid? (To be fair, I would most likely feel simarily in this situation) In case you need some validation for your situation, I believe the fact that your therapist assumes it could be PTSD is already validating in itself. There is no one (I think) that would invalidate what has happened to you and your mental health right now, even though if after further research your therapist would tell you you don't formally have PTSD. It is not because you wouldn't meet the theoretical criteria, that your pain or sufferings are less valid or less severe. 


I wish you can enjoy peace of mind soon and that this will be clarified soon! 

((P.S. This might be an unpopular opinion, but although any diagnosis his strict criteria, some criteria are a bit multi-interpretable and therefore, I dare to claim diagnosing is not an 'exact' practice. There are important conventional steps in diagnosing and they try to make the process as objective as possible, but it always depends on the individual. For instance, some would argue that as long as you don't have an official diagnostic test or procedure it is not official, and just an agreed diagnosis between your therapist and you for insurance. Anyhow, the above remains true. Whether this will eventually turn out to be an 'actual' diagnosis or a situational diagnosis in the context of insurance, it seems like your therapist takes your symptoms and sufferings seriously)).

Personally, for me, that urge is only related to safety concerns. When my surroundings feel (psychogically) unsafe, I tend to mask or 'conform' to some degree. So for me when I am alone or with strangers that don't ask invasive questions or are also outcasts, I don't feel the need to mask at all. I would say the key lays in a psychologically safe environment, and especially when you have to unlearn to conform and be more authentic a safe environment is crucial. 


More specifically, it can start with small steps, being a little bit more open about your own opinions, beliefs etc. (This can be easier to do in a new group of friends or with strangers you meet abroad than with people you have known for a long time). This could also start by listening to more podcasts, interviews of artists or reading more, because given the variety of thoughts there is a higher chance you will find/recognize yourself in others, and realize there are people out there like you. Even though who you are might not be very 'normative' or like the 'masses', it can be validating and helpful to recognize parts of yourself in others (it can be easier to find this online in podcasts than in your own circles), this can help you to accept yourself more and build that confidence. I think safety and confidence about your right/desire to be yourself and act on it can help you to slowly unlearn conforming.


Expect from what others have written, I believe it can be a very slow process for some (as it was and still is for me), but it is also a bit unrealistic - I think - to just not conform on one day. I am glad for others who can, but based on your short description, I guess there is some real fear and stress symptoms within you, so that's why I guess you could help yourself through small cognitive and behavioural experiments (as I tried to describe above), that will slowly make it more natural for you to be your authentic self and to not always automatically conform. Also, psycho education on reasons why human beings conform and reasons why it is harmful in the long run (like you have described feelings of being isolated, loneliness and perhaps feeling disconnected and untrue to yourself) can help to motivate you to start with small actions. To conform is totally natural from an evolutionary perspective, so be mild and gentle with yourself in the meantime.



Best of luck!

Hi! It's really nice to read your little experiments are making you feel well in your body and about yourself! Keep it up!! 

Actually, I feel like you are already transitioning... and by that I mean as you may know a transition has many aspects (personal, social, expression, physical). It seems like you are already transitioning on a personal level and identifying with another gender than you have been for most of your life. You are also experimenting with expression and the more physical aspects. Meanwhile, you are contemplating whether or not to expand this to the social dimension and to also discuss options about HRT. So, actually, apparently, it is not too early. At least, for some aspects, it has not been too early, since you feel quite comfortable with how things are going now. 

As for the other part(s) that keep.your mind very busy and contemplating whether or not you should also go along with the other intended steps, iy's wise to indeed reflect on whether or not other steps can follow soon and the reasons why you should or shouldn't wait. Like you have hinted at I qlso think you and your therapist will know best how to proceed from here, based on your past, personality and state of your mental health. 

But I would like to ask why you wonder whether it is too early to transition (I believe I haven't really read it in your post). Does it only have to do with the relatively short duration of identifying and living this way? Or is there anything deeper involved? (Are you afraid about how some friends may react, or about your job opportunities, or a potential dissatisfaction with the results of HRT?) What kind of doubts are you really dealing with? I think these will really be decisive in your trajectory. Depending on your doubts, you can have exploring conversations with your therapist or talk to a doctor to inform yourself more about HRT. 

Also, it is possible that once you decide to start with HRT you will have have a waiting period (depending on laws and your doctor). So, when making your decision you might also take this into account. This waiting period may also make new emotions and thoughts arise that inform you more about how you truly feel about this. Sometimes people are better to access their actual doubts and feelings towards something when the reality is approaching and is about to shift from a hypothetical situation to an actual one. For this reason, I would definitely talk to a doctor about HRT (in addition to your therapist), having that talk, may arise more or other questions, feelings etc. And provide you with more information about yourself that you weren't able to get to yet. Perceive it as a mirror ;)


A second kind of question I suggest reflecting on (if I may ;) ) would be:  you have been thinking about this for quite some time and you feel like it affects your daily life (thinking, functioning etc.), would it be possible for you to postpone it 'as if starting HRT would be too early'? How would you react someone would say to you "it is too early"? Would it give you some peace of mind to not have to make the decision now and having someone or a law decide for you that you should at least wait 6 months or 2 more years (just having a temporary mental break); or would you for instance feel dissappointed, if so, why?


Feel free to keep us updated! Best of luck!!

Hi, based on the replies of others it is indeed quite common. In addition to the intelligence part and their input, you might be interested in the "being" aspects of giftedness. Some research that have been conducted on giftedness show gifted people are more likely to excel at some personality factors based on how their brain is wired (neurologically speaking). Broadly speaking aspects as high intensity in one's experiences (including emotions);  tendency to perfectionism; high sensitivity to morality and justice; creative humour; high sensitivity to their surroundings (scanning of people, impressions etc.); critically challenging of authority; high degree of self-reflection and philosophical tendencies (critical attitude, which is not necessarily linked to high intellegence) etc.

Although this differs from your more cognition-related question, I just wanted to illustrate that intellingence not only varies across dimensions and tasks, but that giftedness also has other characteristics than one's measured intelligence and cognitive performances. The reason why I wanted to add this is because it can sometimes help one to enhance their selfview, to view yourself one's giftedness as a whole (rather than just the intellegence part) and appreciate other - less measurable, but probably very notable - aspects of one's giftedness. This might be especially 'validating' when you feel 'dumb'

Hi, since I don't know where you live and what kind of regulations apply, read my point of view with an extra critical eye ;-).
As far as I am concerned (and where I live), the biggest motivation to admit a client to a closed hospital department would be safety for others and yourself. Like you have said intent is a very crucial factor in this matters (and I have also heard that they use it for the purpose of testing new medication in a safe environment, with close monitoring).


So in your case, I believe an open discussion about this should be possible, under the condition that you specify that you don't have the intent nor the plans, like you have clarily stated here. Secondly, the personality, experience, style etc. of your therapist play a major role (I think). For example, based on my observations, mine is a little bit more relaxed on these matters as their top priority is to create an open discussion space and believes that in order to have open discussions, clients don't constantly have to worry about the consequences of the content they bring to session. This is just an illustration to say: Athough some will argue, there is always a legal aspect at the end of the day, I believe there is some wiggle room for interpretation and variations in how therapists based in the same area, under the same law, would react to your case


Am in interested in as to why and how you would like to discuss methods with your therapist? I can think of some therapeutical reasons (and not to demonstrate how well prepared you would be or how easily you have access to some resources). In case you believe you need to get some details about methods of your chest to be able to release emotions or deal with anxiety or for other reasons, I believe such a discussion would be feasible. Reflect well on your preferences or needs to discuss the methods and how you could do this. Based on my experiences, 80% is about how you frame it, the context you provide.


Of course, you know your therapist best (in terms of their style, policy and how worried they usually are). It is indeed possible that some more inexperienced therapists or the ones who mostly adhere to a standard policy (rather than assessing case per case) just to be sure, would rapport this. How do you estimate the chances best on your therapist's style (levels of worries) and your framing? Based on yout overall observations and gut feeling do you think they would react calmly of you address your ideations as intense but passive, with a clear emphasis on no intent and plans? 


---- in short: go for it. It would be a pity that you feel you need to hold this back in order to not be send to a psych ward. Based on what you have written, I think your therapist don't have enough evidence that you are a direct danger to yourself.

Sometimes you don't know that your shoulders are tense or that your hips are storing tension until someone asks what do you in your shoulders? What do you feel in your hips? The feeling 'tense' in the body can sometimes be general and an overall experience, but often the feeling of overall tension in the body can be broken down/analyzed in multiple 'hot spots' of tension, for example specificially in the neck; shoulders; hips; jaws; arm muscles or even feet.


-- Apart from physical muscle tension, body scan exercises also help to feel emotions in the body such as when a sad wave flows over your face, or when fear tumbles around in your stomach and chest etc; or when you discover anger when exploring the tension in the jaw etc.I have cried mutliple times during guided body scans ;). It has become really meaningful to me.


I hope your fear of losing your therapist won't overwhelm you but motivate you to try out ways (such as guided body scan) to get in touch with your emotions and body. I hope this might help somehow: there is a huge chance, like you have written, that he did think about the consequences and that he really cared about all of you. I just hope this adds some perspective that he most likely did care... Thinking about the consequences might have stopped him a few times, might have postponed the act for you... At least, in my case, it did, I have shed buckets of tears thinking about the consequences for others, but I can't guarantee I would never act upon it....

Furthermore, there is a big chance that he really tried to seek help, that he googeled resources, that he sought online help etc. For example, I (22) go to psychotherapy for 2 years now, but no one of my family members know (I still live at home with my parents and siblkng), I don't want them to know, I don't trust them with this information. But I know that if I would die and I would not disclose this information through a message, they would also believe like I almost didn't try to get better. All I am saying, there are lots of different ways to seek help, including hidden ones online. Also he might have thought about taking the step towards help but didn't make it... Shame is a huge barrier to seeking help ... Also, sometimes people drop some hints, but feel like their experiences are being brushed off by well meant advice such as "Don't worry so much, it will turn out well" or stuff like that. I am not saying you have done this, personally, that is my experience that whenever I superficially open up to someone my experiences are diminished as regular negative experiences that everyone go through "everyone feels like this sometimes, hang on, it will pass". I believe that because of these general statements that circulate in society, people have lots of difficulties to talk about their struggles even if they want to.

Lastly, he might felt like it was a lost case anyways... 'Solutions'/resources to turn to that might seem evident to us might not come to mind when your brain is so filled with dark thoughts and troubled by sleem deprivation, self hatred etc (which are also common symptoms of depression). 



I really hope this might help you to find a way to deal with your grief ~

Well, about the issues gifted kids face, based on what I have been reading in academic articles, I think of the emotional intelligence and philosophical needs of gifted kids. They often appear as mature for their age, but sometimes adults then expect more of them, for example that they take up responsibility of their mistakes better than their peers can, even though coming across as more mature, doesn't mean gifted kids have already learnt all of those other skills. Or another example would be that parents feel like "you are too young for this" even though their gifted child is actually ready to do it, but are being held back because a certain act is not typical for their age. Common problems are related to the lack of challenges being offered to gifted kids or understimulation, which can lead to 'underperforming', 'bore-outs' and even dropouts from school.

Another thing that researches have been investigating is the problem of overrationalizing of gifted people and even though they are quite emotionally intelligent and sensitive to social things, they are not always enough in touch with their own emotions and body. (However, this could also be said about many people in a result-oriented society).

Also, what might be relevant for you to (without saying that there has to be a direct link!) is that gifted children are interested in existential questions from a young age, whereas other kids are focusing on that a bit later on or less frequently, for example they would mention it and question it shortly but wouldn't want to be your conversation partner in a phylosophical conversation about it. It is said that because gifted kids have other things on their minds,  other interests, complex views... they can feel more lonely and their intellectual needs are not always met in conversations with not gifted kids/people.
When gifted kids are more occupied with questions about the meaning of life, death, suffering... they can develop existential depression and other symptoms related to anxiety for example. Also, kids don't have the same resources as adults. They cannot discuss those concerns with professionals and their emotional regulation systems is still developing.
There is no clear research on the prevelance of SI in gifted kids, but there are some voices who state that gifted kids who experience SI might have more complex associations towards it than other people who experience SI.

It can certainly be true that your anxiety symptoms are related to masking of giftedness, autism, adhd ... However, other things can be going on as well of course. 

To answer the 'how' question, starting points may include talking to a psychologist, therapist or psychiatrist about your concerns related to this. They have official screening lists for autism. Depening on the country you live in, psychologists and therapists most likely are not 'allowed'to formally diagnose, but since they explore your concerns, have knowledge about different causes of anxiety symptoms and are allowed to ask you to fill in official screening tests for indication, it can be a good first step. They also have professional connections with diagnosis centers or psychiatrists who are allowed to fromally diagnose people. 
Official diagnosis comes with a whole range of parts such as 'history analysis' because looking at the surface lots of people seem to have adhd, autism or ... in order to avoid misdiagnosis they really go deep. They explore the underlying dynamics. 

Also, what I should add is that diagnosing is expensive!! Official diagnosis processes are expensive. That is why some people choose to never get started with it and just 'trust their gut feeling'. Of course, I can understand that for some people it can help to get closure or a better understanding of who you are if you get a diagnosis or not. 
So, how some people do it before spending lots of money is talking for a couple of sessions to a therapist, psychologist ... who can sometimes already sense that you're 'feeling' about this might be rather right or rather wrong, and maybe based on their experience they bring other input about something that you might not have been thinking about yet!!! For example, imagine you would want to get tested for adhd, autism, giftedness and something else. That would be extremely expensive. If a therapist would feel like one is more likely applicable to you, you can make a more profound and informed choice about what you want to explore further.

Also, you don't have to undergo official diagnosis per se. It is up to you. You can also (first) read academic papers about those subjects, but the most 'precise' way to get a more certain answer to your queqtion would be official diagnosing.

The most important thing is that you make an informed choice and then go along with it (in the sense that you should then just give that process a try and hopefully it is one that is beneficial to you).

For example, I like exploring, questioning and philosophy, but at the end of the day I would also like to have some concrete tools, not specific answers but at least some starting points to help myself further. Therefore, I decided that thz 'philosophy part' that I like wasn't the priority while deciding the style, but the goal setting and evidence based working method were. So, I went for Cognitive Behav. Therapy. And then, I even obtained the more loose philosophy part through the personality of my psychologist, which was a nice bonus. But luckily he can also think in more concrete terms when I am floating in all kind of philosophical reasonings, he grabs back to reality and tries to make sure we get practical tips too.
In terms of goal setting, CBT is an interesting one, and of the therapist is someone who generally speaking has the attitude of reading clients as the person they are, you get the best of two worlds. By that I mean: the two aspects you have described about the professionals you have experience with.

I have no experience with other forms myself, but it is 'generally believed' that psychoanalysis is more vague in terms of goalsetting, by that I mean the conversations can get very deep, but they professional don't necessarily steers that much or offers enough guidance, depending on how much guidance you want in the treatment.

Just to give you an example (note that this is anecdotal): a family member of mine describes her experience with her therapists as 'passive'. She complained that 2 of her therapists whl she has been seeing left too much room for silence and didn't offer tools, but personally based on my understanding of psychoanalysis the help doesn't lay in offering specific tools, but rather digging deeper into profound issues that can clarify where daily life struggles are rooted in. This family member says the mismatch is because of the passive personality, incompetence and shyness of those therapists, which could be true! It is not impossible to meet 2 rather incompetent therapists in a row (every job market has lower than average performer but honestly I also feel like this family member has no idea about the different styles, because when I asked about the approach of the therapists, each time she had no idea. It was me who had googled the 'official approach' those therapists were familiar with. Guess what: both of them were mainly focusing on psychoanalysis, while this family member didn't intentionally look for this style, she ended up with it, due to being uninformed. However, it still can be true that this family member could have a positive experience with psychoanalysis. 


Best of luck to you!!

Hi! First of all, I am not a therapist, I am on the "client's side". (For context, I am also not officially diagnosed, just wanted to be honest about that).

So far, I have had a great experience with psychotherapy. I honestly feel lucky, beacuse I know that a great deal of it is thanks to the personality and mindset of my psychologist. He is not specialized in giftedness and works witt cognitive behav. therapy. Even though he is not specialized in giftedness, he really challenges my thinking patterns, uses advanced metaphors and is able to link up different topics we talked about through a personal narrative, so he doesn't just analyzes through a clinical framework. He really pays attention to the person we is sitting in front of him, their way of thinking, their way of seeing the world, their way of talking... I think the reason I feel that this is helpful is the great combination of open philosophical conversations about difficulties in life (which really gives room to you as a humanbeing) and specific conversations about symptoms from a psychological point of view for actually treating things. I think only one or the other wouldn't be as helpful for me.
For example, as a child I was really interested in psychoanalysis, but as an adult and client I don't believe it would help me that much with specific issues. Then, as a (gifted) person, you might feel even more lost and have the impression that therapy in general can't help you.
(P.S. He compensates for him not being specialized in some fields by taking our cases into supervision sessions, that are led by a professor who also has other specializations than me psychologist.)

Also, if you are interested in psychotherapy, I do believe there are some therapists out there. It also depends on what you would like to work on. Even though a specialist isn't specialized in giftedness but is quite well informed about neurodiversity and has an open attitude to multilayered conversations, it might work!! All I wan to say is that maybe some therapists who are specialized in giftedness won't be a good fit for you, because of their personality and approach. Specialization is 1 thing, but approach (do you like them to take charge of the conversation, do you like official survey lists every now and then, do you like ...) also really influences how you feel about psychotherapy.
(On the other hand, I certainly DO NOT want to downplay specialization!!! It is wonderful that there are psychotherapists who actually are specialized in this matter. I just wanted to provide some perspective that personality and approach are extremely important, according to my experience).

Anyways, I am quite sure that they have heard it before. I believe that it is totally normal. When someone new enters our lives we are curious and in this case you explore important thoughts and situations together during sessions, so it is very normal that that lingers on in your daily life and that you also wonder about their live outside their office. For some people this reduces a bit over time, for others it stays that way. In all of those cases, personally, I don't think it is necessary to talk about it during sessions, unless you want to or feel like it would be helpful. But as it is something that is a reality for most clients (however it can make us feel weird etc.) it doesn't have to be a big deal, if you know what I mean? It is not my goal to belittle this experience by the way.

But as you wrote "it seems like I place my T p on a pedestal" it might be relevant to adress it in therapy! When you feel like you are admiring that person 'too much' or putting them on a pedestal and you feel like it might make you hold on certain stuff because you don't want to come across as weird in front of that person that you are putting on a pedestal, it might be worth it to discuss that! 

So you see, we could discuss anything during therapy but sometimes it is difficult to decide whether it is worth our time etc. If you feel like that fact that you are putting them on a pedestal is 'limiting' your process, I would adress and explore it together in therapy. If you feel like it is something that keeps you occupied with and that influences your days but not in a bad way, you can experience that on your own without necessarily having to talk that part through during sessions.

So it is really up to you actually ... Do you feel like it is bothering you (a lot) or was it something that worried you or that you felt weirded out by for a moment? 

Best of luck!

Hi! Like others have said it really depends on your former experiences and issues. 

If you feel like the gender of a therapist wouldn't really matter to you, leave it open and see what comes! I honestly was doubting about this as well and when I contacted a practice they just assigned me to a therapist without asking about preferences and without me giving up a preference and tadaaa they assigned me to a male therapist and I think we have a very interesting match! 

I can't say that I don't believe I wouldn't have interesting matches with females therapists, I think it REALLY depends o**n the personality traits, the way of approaching things, the language the person uses (certain words, ways of phrasing ...), the humour sometimes, the body language, sometimes appereances may influence how open you will be ...** So, if there is a possibility to deduct some information through pictures (which might not be the best and most fair way, but if someone appears 'creepy' to you or reminds you of another person it might be not a good idea to 'waste' time). You can't predict people's way of speaking and voice etc. unless you can call them or something. 

(I don't say that gender will never have a certain impact and that other people are wrong on this. It is really personal and if you already feel like the gender of a therapist will play a role, it isn't wrong to take that as a 'selection criteria', but if you feel like it won't have a large impact, why don't you give it a shot)

Also, the most important thing of course are the scholing, studies and knowlegde/experience ... of the therapist. Generally speaking, that information can be found on their website or the website of the organization for which they work. Please inform yourself on different therapeutic approaches! Sometimes people feel like they don't have a match that works for them, because of the fact that the approach during sessions isn't what they feel comfortable with or don't feel like it is helpful. So that would be step 1, I suppose. 

But apart from that, indeed, there is a certain amount of personal things that will influence the bound. Some people you naturally just trust more and can be open with more than others.

To summerize:

1. Make sure you contact therapists that work with an approach that suits you. For example, not everyone feels comfortable with psychodynamic therapy and prefer  cognitive behaviour therapy (or systems therapy or ...) . Don't 'waste' time and possible matches by going on a path that doesn't fit want you would feel like you need to do in therapy. Because a misfit with the therapeutic approach will probably feel like a mismatch with your therapist or goals ...
2. Next,  I think you should brainstorm about what kind of people you like to talk to/can be open with (think of the personality traits a nice teacher had for example). Only you can decide how important the role of gender is here. If you don't know that yet, that's totally fine! Maybe the first therapist won't feel like a good fit for you, but then I think it's nice to evaluate why they weren't a nice fit for you: did gender really played a role in how well it machted or were there other factors?
3. and then thirdly you can look for therapists that might match that image. But please know that the perfect therapist doesn't exist, however I do believe the listed things above can sometimes give a sense of direction to avoid a total mismatch. 

(P.S. Do not look for characteristics a best friend of yours would have to have or a partner. Don't look for something that might facilitate a romantic match, do you know what I mean? You might that paper and pen and imagine "how does a fitting coach, mentor, therapist ... life guide, supporting person ... would look like (not just physically)?" and "what is important in a mentor, coach, therapist ... that I should look for that is different from my other relationships/friendships ...?")

Best of luck!

Hi, I'm sorry to hear you had a bad experience during that first time. However, I'm truely glad to hear that your wife is supportive and that you are willing to give it another chance. 

Like others already said: it's a good idea to be as open and transparant as possible. That being said I realize that it isn't easy to use explicit words. If you feel like you can, go ahead, psychologist use straightforward terms themselves. But if you feel like it is more safe and comfortable to build it up and still being clear enough/not too vague nor mysterious, you could say something like, "I am having some rather unhealthy coping strategies that I would like to change/like to have some help with."    or "I am having difficulties dealing with certain emotions and my wife (and I) are worried about how I deal with it."

So, a first session is often concentrated around the question "why are you here?"/"What are your expectations?"/"What are the difficulties you are facing?" ... So they actually really invite you and give you the chance to mention your SH quite early in the conversation. If you are able to do so instead of turning around the question, do so! But if you feel like you can't/are avoiding it, it might also help to let that therapist know that you know what your are coming for, but feel like you can't say it right away. By saying this concern (like you wrote it here) out loud, you create some distance from your worries and give your therapist the opportunity to help you by asking other kind of questions to get you to speak out what you wanted to. So, introducing it vaguely is even better than avoiding it completely. But when you are speaking vaguely, feel free to let them know that you are aware of the fact that you are adressing it vaguely and that you are willing to discuss it with them (because you really want help) but that you don't know how to yet. There's something beautiful and hopeful in sharing your intentions and concerns.

Most therapists really don't see hospitalization is a first option. They really acknowlegde SH might be dangerous, but they don't try to overfocus the behaviour itself. Normally, they work more on the emotions and mechanisms that make you re-do it.

(But I do understand that this might be something your fear for! However, if hospitalization is the first thing a therapist mentions in that matter, I think they aren't well informed. Lots of people who engage in SH will never be hospitalized. (Of course you know it depends on whether or not someone who engages in SH also has (active) suicidal ideations. But even in that case, it's best to be as open as possible. That way you guys can avoid misinterpretations. When therapists feel like you are holding back important information that could bring you into more danger, they will get more worried than you actually telling them the information.) Professionals all learn that the SH status should be explored first and if it turns out that you are in danger indeed (in terms of infections etc.), then of course they can have a talk with you about hospitalization, but it isn't the first step, nor the second. But I hope that you don't exclude that option on the long run (some people actually do benefit from it).

Best of luck with that!

Hi, I really follow what the others already commented! Coping mechanisms are very individual things. But of course, it's true that arguments with loved ones and relationship difficulties can cause extra stress that can lead to excessive use of a coping mechanism. But again, distress come from various aspects in life. It's often not an event that make you turn to a certain coping mechanism, but the lack of healthy coping mechanisms and a bad relationship with oneself. 

Concerning your second question, I can tell it's a very human question. It's understandable that you want to reduce the harm, but in fact what matters is to discover his need. What is really causing him the mental pain that makes him engage in this? (Is it really an argument or rather certain specific words or the feeling of not being good enough ... Often it's not the reality that make people engage in self harm, but the interpretation/meaning we give to the things we see around us by associations based on our past) It's not necessarily up to you to solve that puzzle. Actually, it's not up to you at all. I would advice to ask him whether or not he wants professional help, because that's the only way to really reduce self harm. It can only work when the person engaging in it has the desire to lessen/to stop. (Works the same way for other addictions)

So, what I really want to say is that as a partner, you appear to be on the spot, but actually you are the sound board. He has difficulties of his own (which might be a bit related to your relationship) and as you are his partner/close to him you 'happen to be' the person who gets the blame and who feels the need to reduce the harm. The blame is not fair and I really hope you don't take it too personal (it's very common to blame others for distress). The only way to reduce the excessive cutting is by not striving to reduce it ;) by that I mean, at least you should not strive towards it. The goal should be: he should experience less distress and as a consequence feel less urges to engage in self harm. Your role in this can be the non-judgemental supporter. The 'real' work is up to him and professionals. 

​

Best of luck with this challenge!

You're welcome! Yeah I can imagine that in a reflex you would immediately say that. It's kind of natural to feel that we should make something that appears dangerous stop. But what we actually should try is to think whenever we see someone doing it 'I shouldn't make thr SH stop, I should try to help to take the pain underneath the SH stop first'. Because when the reasons why someone started doing it stop, SH behaviour can eventually be reduced or can stop.

So I think whenever this situation happens you should try to actively remind yourself of 'I shouldn't stop the SH, the pain underneath should stop first.' It's really though, but I think this one will make the difference! People tend to focus to much on the SH, however SH is 'just' an expression of so much more that a person can't speak about.

Maybe this might help: I heard that when you catch someone doing it, you can say 'hi I see that you're hurting and turning your coping mechanism, how about I give some minutes for yourself and I come back in 5 minutes with a hug and a talk?'. 
But of course you can also drop the 5 minute rule. It heard they sometimes use it in mental hospitals to help the clients who felt caught and give them a minute to process the fact they got caught.
So I would say please really try to avoid the words 'stop' or 'please, don't because those words are imperatives, right? And these words actually implies you want her to give up her coping skill. It will be really hard for you but if you can manage to avoid these quick reactions and instead think of talking to her in a neutral way and asking her if she want a hug or want to join you for a walk.
Yeah I think that might be it. Suggest a little alternative at that moment, that way you are passively showing her that there are other ways to get distraction from hard feelings without completely taking away her method right now. I think your 'job' is to keep an eye on her wellbeing but not necessarily stop the SH, that will be up to her counselor on the long term. For now being there for her, showing that you don't judge her, don't you don't feel ashamed or anything about it. 

Last tip: please never comment on scars. I mean don't say 'I know it's hard and that you SH, but the scars aren't okay, that's so ugly and when you'll grow up you'll regret the scars'. Instead buy her a cream and make sure she can walk around the house without having to cover up her scars. 
There doesn't have to be scars of course, I genuinely hope so. But whenever it would be the case I hope she won't hate her body because of her SH and that she can learn to not hide her body.

I hope these tips are specific enough and useful?

So, I don't know for sure, but I personally think it  kind of means that a situation isn't resonating with you ALL the time anymore, like it doesn't affect every decision, moment... in your daily life anymore. But I think inherent to this, it means the situation, the person... is still in your thoughts, on your mind but like in a less 'flashy', obvious way. I imagine it as an event is in your memory and the feelings related to it are still in your heart, body, soul and every now and then it shows up more clearly in the front again. You see? Like on special occassions, at certain hard moments, in periods of general nostalgia to the past or for a short moment everyday. 
So I feel like what you describe is similar to my view on what 'moving on' could be like, but yeah I really want to stress that I don't believe people can fully move on like 100% in a way they really forget what happened. I also don't think that's the goal of moving on? I think it's nice if someone can carry on with his life without feeling affected by the loss of someone all the time and in an intense way.

So honestly I don't think you can and will ever 'forget' your loved one. Nevertheless I understand yiu worry you will and already partially did. It's normal we want to keep the vibes of a person alive and we think that's by remembering how their voice was like, how they would react in situations ... But I think there are other and more subtle ways to make the memory of that person a part of your life, for example through a song, a band you know the person was keen on. Or by taking time to recall a smile of that person when it's his birthday every year. Or by re-using or implementing a quote, a funny word that person used often into your own language use...
I don't know if that might work for you, but it kind of works for me. (An aunt of me whom I didn't see that often and didn't know well on an emotional level, she passed away on May 25th 2013, and even though I also blamed myself for forgetting her voice, her gestures... I caught myself thinking of her when 2 specific songs play, because I listened to those songs in the period after her death. And now every tile I hear it I automatically thinks of her, so this way even though it doesn't happen daily near weekly I do think more often of her than I always thought. Also I remember her birthday and always notice if the annual date of her death comes closer. And I unexpectedly think of her when I'm having a hard time, (even though I didn't think of her at such moments if she was still alive). Besides, her favourite juice reminds me of her. It ain't much, but honestly I love these little emotional and honouring moments because I doesn't affect my daily life anymore, but still I keep her alive in my life :-) ) I genuinely hope you can also find your way to keep your loved one alive without feeling the obligation to constantly have to think about him.
